proposals.label: Sansbury et al. (2015)
proposals.rationale: The entry currently records only neonatal-onset diabetes and has no RFX6 variants. Sansbury et al. (2015) describe 2 cousins with RFX6-confirmed Mitchell-Riley syndrome whose diabetes began in childhood (ages 3 and 6 years), and both were alive at 9 years. The paper also adds 2 new RFX6 nonsense mutations (R726X and R866X), a proposed genotype-phenotype correlation based on whether the mutant transcript escapes nonsense-mediated decay, carrier data that do not support a diabetes risk in heterozygotes, and a recommendation on genetic testing.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome whose diabetes was diagnosed at ages 3 and 6 years, not in the neonatal period. The first, a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation, had duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and a Meckel diverticulum. She had hyperglycemia at age 2 years and presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at age 3 years. Her insulin and C-peptide levels were very low and her autoantibodies were negative. She also had an absent gallbladder and gastrointestinal bleeding due to gastric heterotopia in the small bowel. Her cousin, a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation, had duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia at age 5 years, was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6 years, and had chronic iron deficiency anemia. Neither child had liver disease, and both were alive at age 9 years.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) studied 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes. Using targeted next-generation sequencing of neonatal diabetes genes, with Sanger confirmation, they identified compound heterozygous nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene in both cousins: R726X in exon 17 and R866X in exon 18. The fathers were heterozygous for R726X and the mothers carried R866X, and the mutations were traced back to the grandmothers. The authors predicted that R726X would be subject to nonsense-mediated decay. They predicted that R866X would escape it and would yield a partially truncated protein that keeps the entire DNA-binding domain. These were the first RFX6 mutations reported in exons 9 to 19.

proposals.citation: Pearl EJ, Jarikji Z, Horb ME. Functional analysis of Rfx6 and mutant variants associated with neonatal diabetes. Dev Biol 351: 135-45, 2011. [PubMed: 21215266]
proposals.label: Pearl et al. (2011)
proposals.rationale: The entry has no functional or animal-model evidence for RFX6 and an empty variant table. Pearl et al. (2011) gave the first in vivo functional proof: in Xenopus, three patient RFX6 mutations (R181Q, S217P and an exon 7 truncation) failed to rescue the rfx6 knockdown phenotype. Rfx6 knockdown abolished pancreatic and endocrine gene expression, but the gall bladder was unaffected.

paragraphs.text: Pearl et al. (2011) tested 3 of the 4 homozygous RFX6 mutations previously identified in patients with Mitchell-Riley syndrome in a Xenopus rescue assay. None of the mutant constructs could rescue the rfx6 morpholino knockdown phenotype, whereas wildtype rfx6 did. The first was an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) substitution in the DNA-binding domain (n = 16; 3 normal, 4 moderate, 9 severe). Based on the structure of the DNA-bound RFX1 DNA-binding domain, this residue makes direct contact with the X-box DNA, so R181Q introduces a charge reversal at a key DNA-binding residue. The second was a ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution C-terminal to the DNA-binding domain, in a domain of unknown function (n = 16; 2 moderate, 14 severe). The authors noted that proline residues can introduce kinks into proteins and disrupt their structure. The third was a truncation after exon 7 that retained the DNA-binding domain but lacked the dimerization domain (n = 16; 1 normal, 1 moderate, 14 severe). Its failure to rescue was consistent with an inability to dimerize, since RFX transcription factors bind as homo- or heterodimers. The authors concluded that these mutations have an in vivo effect and that mutant RFX6 is responsible for at least some of the defects in Mitchell-Riley syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Pearl et al. (2011) cloned the Xenopus laevis rfx6 homolog. Its protein shares 69% amino acid identity with human RFX6, and its RFX DNA-binding domain is identical to the human domain. Rfx6 was expressed in 2 phases: broadly throughout the anterior endoderm from stage NF15 to NF34, and then in a punctate pattern in endocrine cells of the gut and pancreas from NF40. Morpholino knockdown of rfx6 had no effect at gastrula and neurula stages. From NF25 it reduced expression of hnf6 and foxa2, and by NF35 it reduced expression of all anterior endodermal markers (hnf6, pdx1, ptf1a), with complete loss of insulin expression. In morphant tadpoles, pancreatic pdx1, ptf1a, elastase and insulin expression was almost completely abolished, and no glucagon, somatostatin or neuroD expression was detected in the gastrointestinal tract. A hormone-inducible wildtype rfx6 construct (100 pg rfx6-GR) partially rescued elastase expression (n = 36; 20 normal, 15 moderate, 1 severe) compared with morpholino alone (n = 47; 6 moderate, 41 severe). Rescue occurred only when dexamethasone was added at NF25; earlier induction produced a gain-of-function phenotype. Microarray analysis of morphant anterior foregut at NF30, NF40 and NF44 showed downregulation of pancreas, stomach, intestine, heart and lung genes and upregulation of kidney marker genes. These results were confirmed for agr2, frp5, surfactant C, nkx2.5 and kcnj1. The gall bladder was unaffected in morphants, with normal gall bladder expression of hnf6 (17 of 18) and sox17-alpha (18 of 20); hnf6 was reduced in the duodenum. Expression of the liver marker hex was unaffected, although the liver appeared smaller. This contrasts with the frequent gall bladder involvement in the human syndrome.

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) cloned the Xenopus laevis homologue of rfx6 and found that the Xenopus Rfx6 protein shares 69% amino acid identity with human Rfx6, with an RFX DNA-binding domain identical to the human DNA binding domain; rfx6 was expressed in two phases, broadly throughout the anterior endoderm from NF15 to NF34 and later in a punctate fashion in endocrine cells of the gut and pancreas beginning at NF40.
quotes: The Xenopus Rfx6 protein shares 69% amino acid identity with human Rfx6, 68% with mouse and 63% with zebrafish. The Xenopus RFX domain is identical to the human DNA binding domain (DBD), and only one and two amino acids different to the mouse and zebrafish DBDs, respectively.
In the first phase, rfx6 expression was found throughout the anterior endoderm in a broad domain from NF15 until NF34.
In the second phase, rfx6 was expressed in a punctate fashion throughout the gut and developing pancreas beginning at NF40, similar to that seen for other endocrine markers (Fig. 1E–H).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) showed by morpholino knockdown of rfx6 in Xenopus embryos that loss of rfx6 had no effect on early gastrula and neurula stages, but from NF25 caused reduced expression of hnf6 and foxa2 and by NF35 reduced expression of all anterior endodermal markers (hnf6, pdx1, ptf1a) with complete loss of insulin expression; in tadpoles, pancreatic pdx1 and ptf1a expression was almost completely abolished, as was elastase and insulin, and no glucagon, somatostatin or neuroD expression was detected in the gastrointestinal tract.
quotes: However, beginning at NF25 we observed reduced expression of hnf6 and foxa2, but normal expression of hex, sizzled and sox17α (Fig. 2D–G, and data not shown). By NF35, expression of all anterior endodermal markers (hnf6, pdx1 and ptf1a) were reduced (Fig. 2H–K).
However, in embryos injected with Rfx6 MO1 we did not detect any insulin expression (Fig. 2O).

Within the pancreas, expression of the pancreatic transcription factors pdx1 and ptf1a was almost completely abolished, as was expression of the differentiation markers elastase and insulin (Fig. 3A–J). In addition, we did not detect expression of any endocrine markers (glucagon, somatostatin or neuroD) within the gastrointestinal tract (Fig. 3K–P).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) demonstrated specificity of the knockdown by rescuing the rfx6 morphant phenotype with a hormone-inducible wild-type rfx6 construct: 100 pg of rfx6-GR partially restored elastase expression (n=36, 20 normal, 15 moderate, 1 severe) compared with MO2 alone (n=47, 6 moderate, 41 severe), but only when dexamethasone was added at NF25, with earlier induction producing a gain-of-function phenotype.
quotes: When embryos were injected with MO2, elastase expression was reduced (n=47, 6 moderate, 41 severe), while in embryos co-injected with 100 pg of rfx6-GR and induced at NF25, elastase expression was partially restored (n=36, 20 normal, 15 moderate, 1 severe) (Fig. 4).
Specifically, we found that Rfx6-GR could only rescue the morphant phenotype when dexamethasone was added at NF25; earlier induction resulted in a gain-of-function phenotype.

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) tested three of the four homozygous RFX6 mutations previously identified in patients with Mitchell-Riley syndrome in a Xenopus rescue assay and found that none of the mutant constructs (R181Q in the DNA-binding domain, S217P C-terminal to the DNA-binding domain, and a truncation after exon 7 lacking the dimerization domain) could rescue the rfx6 morpholino knockdown phenotype, whereas wild-type rfx6 did; the authors concluded that these mutations have an in vivo effect and that mutated rfx6 is responsible for at least some of the defects associated with Mitchell-Riley syndrome.
quotes: We also examined whether the mutations found in rfx6 in Mitchell-Riley patients were functional in vivo by testing the ability of three of the four homozygous mutations to rescue the morpholino phenotype. We found that none of these mutant constructs (R181Q, S217P and the exon 7 truncation) were sufficient to attenuate Rfx6 function in vivo (Fig. 5). This strongly suggests that mutated rfx6 is responsible for at least some of the defects associated with Mitchell-Riley syndrome.

Taken together these results show that, unlike the wild-type Rfx6, these mutant constructs were unable to rescue the morphant phenotype, which suggests that these specific mutations identified in Mitchell-Riley patients do have an in vivo effect and contribute to disease progression.

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) reported that co-injection of 100 pg of R181Q mRNA failed to rescue the rfx6 knockdown phenotype (n=16, 3 normal, 4 moderate, 9 severe), and noted that this residue lies in the DNA-binding domain and, based on the structure of the DNA-bound human RFX1 DNA-binding domain, makes direct contact with the DNA of the X-box, so that R181Q introduces a charge reversal in a key DNA-binding residue.
quotes: The first mutation we tested was the R181Q mutation, which lies in the DNA-binding domain (DBD), and based on the structure of DNA-bound human RFX1 DBD this residue makes direct contact with the DNA of the X-box. The R181Q mutant introduces a charge reversal in a key DNA-binding residue. Co-injection of 100 pg R181Q mRNA did not rescue the knockdown phenotype (Fig. 5, n=16, 3 normal, 4 moderate, 9 severe).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) found that the S217P mutant, located C-terminal to the DNA-binding domain in a domain of unknown function, was unable to rescue the rfx6 knockdown phenotype (n=16, 2 moderate, 14 severe); the authors noted that proline residues can introduce kinks into proteins and disrupt their structure.
quotes: The second mutation tested, S217P, is located C-terminal to the DBD in an unknown functional domain; however, proline residues can introduce kinks into proteins and disrupt their structure. Co-injection of 100 pg of S217P was also unable to rescue the knockdown phenotype (Fig. 5E, n=16, 2 moderate, 14 severe).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) showed that an exon 7 truncation mutant of rfx6, which retains the DNA-binding domain but lacks the dimerization domain, also failed to rescue the morphant phenotype (n=16, 1 normal, 1 moderate, 14 severe), consistent with an inability to functionally dimerize, as RFX transcription factors bind as homo- or heterodimers.
quotes: The third mutant construct we tested was the exon 7 truncation mutant, which still contains the DBD, but lacks the dimerization domain. RFX transcription factors are known to bind as homo- or heterodimers to alter gene expression and the expected inability of the exon 7 mutant to functionally dimerize appears to affect the function of Rfx6 as co-injection of 100 pg of the exon 7 mutant also did not rescue the morphant phenotype (Fig. 5E, n=16, 1 normal, 1 moderate, 14 severe).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) performed microarray analysis of anterior foregut tissue from rfx6 morphant and control Xenopus tadpoles at NF30, NF40 and NF44 and found downregulation of pancreas, stomach, intestine, heart and lung genes with an increase in kidney marker genes; results were confirmed by RT-PCR and in situ hybridization showing reduced stomach markers agr2 and frp5, reduced lung marker surfactant C and heart marker nkx2.5, and increased kidney marker kcnj1.
quotes: In general, the microarray results concurred with our phenotypic characterization showing down-regulation of pancreas, stomach, intestine, heart and lung genes, whereas results for liver marker genes was inconclusive. Interestingly, the microarray data did show an increase in kidney marker genes (Table 1).

Stomach markers agr2 and frp5 were reduced, as was the lung marker surfactant C, and the heart marker nkx2.5 (Fig. 7A–H). In contrast, we found increased expression of kidney marker kcnj1, confirming the results observed in the microarray (Fig. 7I,J).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) found that in rfx6 morphant Xenopus the gall bladder was unaffected, with normal gall bladder expression of hnf6 and sox17alpha (reduced in duodenum but not gall bladder, 17/18; sox17alpha normal in 18/20), and that liver marker hex expression was unaffected although the liver appeared smaller; they included these markers because the gall bladder is often affected in Mitchell-Riley syndrome.
quotes: Last, we also found that the gall bladder was unaffected, as the gall bladder component of hnf6 and sox17α expression was normal (Fig. 7M–P). Although expression of these markers was not changed in the microarray we included them in our in situ analysis because the gall bladder is often affected in Mitchell-Riley syndrome.
Although expression of liver marker hex seemed unaffected by the loss of rfx6, the liver did appear smaller (Fig. 7K,L).

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) described Mitchell-Riley syndrome as a recently described neonatal diabetes syndrome in which patients have severe neonatal diabetes and a hypoplastic pancreas accompanied by duodenal or jejunal atresia and a small or absent gall bladder, with patients typically diagnosed within the first week of life and generally dying within their first year of life.
quotes: Mitchell-Riley is a recently described neonatal diabetes syndrome in which patients have severe neonatal diabetes and hypoplastic pancreas accompanied by duodenal or jejunal atresia and a small or absent gall bladder.

Patients with this syndrome are typically diagnosed within the first week of life and generally die within their first year of life. The early onset and severity of disease suggests that in patients with Mitchell-Riley syndrome the pancreas does not develop appropriately in utero.

evidence.statement: Pearl et al. (2011) proposed on the basis of the biphasic rfx6 expression pattern and their functional analyses that Rfx6 has both early and late functions: an early broad role essential for development of most anterior endodermal organs, and a later function restricted to endocrine cells; because Rfx6-GR could rescue only when induced at NF25 and because pdx1 and hnf6 expression were decreased in the loss of function, they placed Rfx6 upstream of pdx1 and ngn3, in contrast to mouse and zebrafish studies placing it downstream of Ngn3.
quotes: Based on the different rfx6 expression patterns and our functional analyses, we propose that rfx6 has both early and late functions. In early development Rfx6 plays a broad role, being essential for development of most anterior endodermal organs. At later stages however, Rfx6 function is restricted to endocrine cells.

Our results differ from that seen in mice and zebrafish where Rfx6 was placed downstream of the transcription factor Neurogenin 3 (Ngn3), which is essential for development of endocrine cells. Our results however, place Rfx6 upstream of Ngn3.
The fact that pdx1 expression is decreased both in our loss-of-function study and the knockout mouse suggests that rfx6 lies upstream of pdx1, and hence also ngn3.

(2010) identified biallelic RFX6 mutations in 5 of 6 probands, found by homozygosity mapping and sequencing, and supported them with EMSA and RNA studies, a knockout mouse, and a genotype-phenotype correlation. paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) sequenced the 19 exons and splice junctions of RFX6 directly. They found missense, splicing, or frameshift mutations in 5 of 6 available probands with the syndrome, and all mutations were inherited from carrier parents. Proband 1, the child of first cousins, was homozygous for a splice donor mutation in intron 2 (IVS2+2T-C). RT-PCR of RNA from the patient's autopsy pancreas detected no properly spliced RFX6 transcript. No RNA was detected from exons 1 and 2, which the authors attributed probably to nonsense-mediated decay. Proband 4 was homozygous for an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7. Proband 5 was homozygous for an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) mutation that affects a highly conserved arginine in the DNA-binding domain; in EMSA this mutation completely abolished DNA binding. Proband 3 was compound heterozygous for 2 splice mutations: loss of the donor site in intron 6 (IVS6+2T-G) and disruption of the acceptor site in intron 1 (IVS1-12A-G).

Pancreas size was somewhat reduced, but exocrine pancreatic enzymes were not deficient. Autopsy in 2 cases showed normal-appearing exocrine pancreas with clusters of chromogranin A-positive cells but no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. The syndrome also included a hypoplastic gallbladder and intractable diarrhea that did not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement.

In addition, the syndrome involves hypoplastic gall bladder, and intractable diarrhea unresponsive to pancreatic enzyme replacement.

proposals.rationale: The paper adds an RFX6 mutation, homozygous R181W, found in a consanguineous family in which it segregated; the entry's variant table currently has no variants. It also adds features the entry does not list: transient neonatal cholestasis with biliary duct dilation, possible ectopic perijejunal pancreatic tissue, and chronic diarrhea and malabsorption that did not respond to exocrine pancreatic supplementation.

paragraphs.text: Zegre Amorim et al. (2015) reported a girl born to first-cousin Gipsy parents. Prenatal ultrasound showed intrauterine growth restriction and a 'double bubble.' She was born at 35 weeks with weight, length, and head circumference below the 3rd centile. She developed hyperglycemia on day 2 and needed continuous insulin. On day 3, insulin and C-peptide levels were very low, and GAD, islet cell, and IA-2 autoantibodies were negative. Laparotomy on day 4 confirmed type II duodenal atresia with annular pancreas, malrotation, and gallbladder agenesis. From day 6 she had cholestasis (conjugated bilirubin 3.07 mg/dL, GGT 458 IU/L), which resolved without treatment by 2 months of age. Ultrasound showed biliary duct dilation and a disproportionately large pancreatic head; the pancreatic tail could not be identified. At surgery, perijejunal submucosal tissue that looked like ectopic pancreatic tissue was seen. The authors described this as a novel feature, but the tissue was not biopsied. She had chronic diarrhea and malabsorption that did not respond to exocrine pancreatic supplementation. At 7 months she had failure to thrive and still depended on insulin and partial parenteral nutrition. Her mother had previously had 3 first-trimester spontaneous abortions and a child with isolated congenital anorectal malformation.

paragraphs.text: Concepcion et al. (2014) described a male infant born at 34 weeks' gestation to nonconsanguineous Vietnamese parents. Before birth he had intrauterine growth restriction and duodenal atresia. He was small for gestational age (birth weight 1375 g). Within 24 hours of birth he had severe hyperglycemia (446 mg/dL), which required an insulin infusion. C-peptide, amylase, lipase, and stool pancreatic elastase were all low. Laparotomy on day 5 confirmed duodenal atresia, intestinal malrotation, and jejunal perforation, and ultrasound suggested an annular pancreas. His later course included cholestatic jaundice, recurrent infections, and feeding intolerance. He also had severe chronic diarrhea that required intermittent parenteral nutrition and did not improve with pancreatic enzymes. Laparotomy at 3 months showed gallbladder agenesis. A hepatobiliary scan did not visualize the gallbladder or the common bile duct, and liver biopsy showed bile ductular proliferation. He developed liver failure and died of sepsis at 5 months of age while awaiting liver transplantation.

Two analysis tools (www.fruitfly.org/seq_tools/splice.html and www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/NetGene2/) predicted that the mutant sequence is no longer likely to be used as a 5’ donor splice site.
The fact that this RFX6 variant is not present in publically available repositories (1000 genomes, dbSNP) suggests that it is rare and that the parents of the proband may be distantly related.

evidence.statement: In a review of 8 patients with RFX6 mutations, Concepcion et al. (2014) noted that the 2 longest survivors were a compound heterozygote with 2 splice site mutations and a patient with a homozygous missense mutation that reduced but did not abolish DNA binding. These 2 patients also had the highest birth weights. In contrast, the authors' patient had disease as severe as patients with homozygous splice site, frameshift, or DNA-binding-abolishing mutations. They noted that chronic diarrhea had been reported in most patients with RFX6 mutations.
quotes: The longest surviving case (Proband 3, alive at 9 years), was the only compound heterozygote, with two different splice site mutations, while the next oldest (Proband 2, alive at 6 years) had a homozygous missense mutation that was shown to reduce but not abrogate DNA binding.
This genotype-phenotype correlation is also reflected in the birth weights of these two cases being the highest of any reported.
Although chronic diarrhea has been reported in the majority of cases with RFX6 mutations (Table 1), it has not been emphasized as a consistent feature of the syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Chandra et al. (2014) found RFX6 in adult human pancreatic endocrine cells. In the human beta-cell line EndoC-betaH2, RFX6 regulated insulin gene transcription, insulin content, and insulin secretion. Knocking down RFX6 lowered expression of calcium-channel genes and reduced L-type calcium-channel activity, which suppressed depolarization-evoked insulin exocytosis. The authors concluded that RFX6 regulates insulin secretion by modulating calcium homeostasis in human beta cells.
